title: LAARMA AI roadside alerts cut cassowary road deaths in Queensland trial
summary: TMR three-month trial at Kuranda: 97% cassowary detection, drivers slowed 6.6 km/h, fatal crashes down 31% (reported 30 July 2025).
account: The Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA) was developed by the University of Sydney's Australian Centre for Robotics and QUT's CARRS-Q with the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads under an iMOVE project; it uses a machine-learning pipeline to detect large animals up to 200 m away and triggers roadside variable message signs. The ABC reported on 30 July 2025 that TMR had used the AI for three months at a busy cassowary crossing on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, Far North Queensland (trial dates not given, so the report date is used), whereas the consortium's iMOVE project page describes a five-month field trial, three months of data collection followed by two months of on-road trialling. TMR told the ABC that the system identified cassowaries with 97 percent accuracy, that drivers slowed by an average of 6.6 km/h at the flashing sign and that fatal crashes fell 31 percent during the trial; the iMOVE page reports speed reductions averaging 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two test sites and gives no collision figure. About two dozen cassowaries were killed on Queensland roads the previous year.
purpose: Detect large animals near the road in real time and warn drivers via variable message signs to reduce animal-vehicle collisions.
system: Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA)
developer: University of Sydney Australian Centre for Robotics and QUT CARRS-Q
deployer: Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads
taxonomy_note: The crashes cut are vehicle strikes on an endangered bird, so the gain is shared with conservation.

ratings.reason: General benefit without an event: trial-level aggregate (speed reduction, 31 percent fewer fatal crashes) with no discrete attributable event.
General benefit without an event: aggregate program result reported by the operating agency.
General benefit without an event: aggregate result over a three-month trial; baseline and statistical detail not published.

ai_role.statement: Machine-learning detection of cassowaries activated the warning signs; TMR attributes the speed reduction and the 31 percent fall in fatal crashes to the system, but the figures are trial aggregates without a peer-reviewed analysis: the 31 percent figure is reported only by the ABC citing TMR, and the consortium's project page reports detection and speed results without a collision figure.
